dek_candidates: A Mumbai contractor that builds railway works, bridges and roads, and runs a concrete plant in Thane — what its DRHP discloses about the offer, the five-year numbers and the risks.
Two segments, one customer that supplied 57% of FY2018 revenue, and an issue price the filing leaves blank. The DRHP explained, page by page.
design_notes: Convert every lakh figure to ₹ crore (divide by 100) in the prose, and say once at the top of the financials section that the filing reports in ₹ lakhs.
State redactions plainly as 'not disclosed' — the issue price ₹[●] and the general corporate purposes amount — and never estimate a substitute figure.
Treat the peer-comparison page as a limitation, not a section: explain the blank price, note what the page does and does not carry, then stop.
Keep the risks section at exactly five items; each one must name a figure or a named counterparty. Do not pad with general IPO boilerplate.
The filing's own competitive-strengths language is promotional in register; attribute such claims to the filing rather than adopting them as the report's voice.
No verdict, no price target, no listing-gain language anywhere. The report ends on the last specific risk, not a summary paragraph.
Expand acronyms at first use in-line: MCGM, MRVCL, MMRDA, DFCCIL, RMC — as clauses in the sentence, not as a glossary block.

beats.beat: The infrastructure half of the business is four kinds of work: railway platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and track laying; bridge contracts across beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss types; bituminous and concrete road construction; and the concrete supply from its own plant.

Work is won by tender, not negotiated: the client floats the tender, holds a pre-bid meeting, contractors bid, the job goes to the lowest quote with a Letter of Acceptance issued to the lowest bidder, and the winner then deposits a performance guarantee before site handover.

That lowest-bid mechanic is the most important thing to understand about the revenue line: the company does not set its price, and the filing says performance could suffer if most bids are not accepted or if it negotiates a lower bid value.
The footprint is Mumbai first, Maharashtra later — the filing describes the company as a major player in Mumbai infrastructure that is consolidating its position in the state.
The concrete plant at Kashimira in Thane district is the only facility the filing describes in any detail, with machinery and quality-control systems attached to the ready mix concrete activity.

The disclosed customer list is short and mostly public: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India, plus private names Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.
Western Railway is both the oldest relationship — a client since 2006 — and the largest exposure: 52% of orders on hand, against 57% of FY2018 revenue from key customers overall.
The filing presents Box Pushing — used for executing projects under live conditions — as a technical differentiator, and cites founders with more than 20 years in the infrastructure industry.
The filing excerpts do not split revenue between the infrastructure segment and the concrete plant, so the reader cannot tell from these pages how much of the business the Thane facility actually is.

business.heading: What the company does
business.purpose: Explain the two-segment contractor model, the tender mechanism that produces the revenue, the operating footprint, and the two concentrations that define the business.

beats.beat: The filing reports in ₹ lakhs, so every figure below is converted to ₹ crore by dividing by 100. Revenue from operations, as restated, runs: FY2014 ₹86.61 crore, FY2015 ₹90.21 crore, FY2016 ₹74.53 crore, FY2017 ₹73.44 crore, FY2018 ₹60.53 crore.
The filing's own summary is blunt about the direction: revenue fell from ₹9,021.12 lakhs in FY2015 to ₹6,053.05 lakhs in FY2018, a decline in a market the same document describes as expanding.
EBITDA — profit before interest, depreciation and tax — was ₹7.84 crore in FY2014, ₹9.46 crore in FY2015, ₹7.83 crore in FY2016, ₹6.76 crore in FY2017 and ₹9.29 crore in FY2018.
Read those two lines together and the interesting fact is the divergence: earnings rose to their second-highest level of the five years in FY2018, the same year revenue fell to its lowest.

Net profit after adjustments was ₹0.96 crore in FY2014, ₹0.78 crore in FY2015, ₹0.33 crore in FY2016, ₹0.16 crore in FY2017 and ₹3.15 crore in FY2018; the filing describes the last year as a sharp increase, from ₹15.86 lakhs to ₹314.66 lakhs.

The FY2018 profit jump is not explained on these pages, and it arrives in the same year revenue hit a five-year low — a question for the reader to carry into the RHP rather than a trend to extrapolate.

The balance sheet is a working-capital balance sheet. Total assets were ₹70.62 crore in FY2014, ₹72.67 crore in FY2015, ₹62.95 crore in FY2016, ₹75.37 crore in FY2017 and ₹82.32 crore in FY2018, against FY2018 revenue of ₹60.53 crore.

The asset base grew in four of five years even as revenue shrank — the filing's own summary of the balance sheet is that shorter-term borrowings rose from ₹3,082.27 lakhs in FY2014 to ₹3,537.35 lakhs in FY2018.

On the debt stack: long-term borrowings fell from ₹6.73 crore in FY2015 to ₹1.33 crore in FY2018, while short-term borrowings across the same period ran ₹32.28 crore, ₹30.21 crore, ₹33.12 crore and ₹35.37 crore — the funding has moved to the short end.
Separately, the company had ₹405.02 lakhs (₹4.05 crore) of unsecured loans outstanding at March 31, 2018, repayable on demand.

Cash generation is the soft spot: the filing states the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years, that sustained negative cash flow could hurt the business, and that failing to recover from sundry debtors on time could affect its financial condition. The cash flow statement figures themselves are not in these excerpts.

financials.heading: Five years of restated numbers
financials.purpose: Tell the financial story in one arc — shrinking revenue, a sudden profit jump, and a balance sheet funded at the short end — with every figure in ₹ crore across all reported periods.

beats.beat: Amit Bholanath Mishra is the promoter and managing director, holding 74,95,476 equity shares — 90.949% of the pre-issue issued, subscribed and paid-up capital.
The remaining directors hold 300 shares each — Bharat kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — while key management personnel Hatim Sakerwala holds 9% of the equity shares.
The filing excerpts do not state the promoter's shareholding after the issue, so the post-issue float cannot be worked out from these pages.

The key management is young relative to the business: chief financial officer Anchal Pachori is 28 and a chartered accountant, and company secretary and compliance officer Mohit Soni is 26 and an associate member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.

Related-party flows are disclosed. In FY2018 the company took ₹68.4 lakhs of loans from key management personnel or board members, paid ₹57.7 lakhs in director remuneration, and carried ₹324.3 lakhs of outstanding payables to related parties as at March 31, 2018.
The company, its promoter and its directors are parties to litigation pending at various stages; the filing does not quantify the claims or name the forums in these excerpts.

On the clean side of the ledger: no director appears on the RBI list of willful defaulters, no criminal cases or investigations are recorded against any director, and the promoter confirms he has not been declared a willful defaulter by the RBI or any other government authority.

Two promoter-linked companies were struck off by the Registrar of Companies for non-operation of business — Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited on March 12, 2016 and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited on March 11, 2016.
The filing also flags that no independent agency has appraised the proposed project, and that no monitoring agency will track how the proceeds are spent.

governance.heading: Who controls it, and the flags
governance.purpose: Show the ownership concentration, the related-party flows, the pending litigation and the specific governance disclosures the filing makes.

beats.beat: Infrastructure here means power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure development — the physical build-out of the country, which is the market the company sells into.

The filing calls that market highly fragmented, working-capital intensive, and worth roughly 8% of India's GDP at constant prices — three phrases that describe A B Infrabuild's own balance sheet as neatly as the industry's.

The demand story is a government spending story: infrastructure spending was assumed at 9.0% of GDP in the 12th Five-Year Plan, and the filing cites an infrastructure investment requirement of ₹50 trillion (US$777.73 billion) by 2022.

The named programmes behind that spending are the 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All; FDI norms were eased in 15 sectors including construction, and the sector drew US$24.67 billion of FDI between April 2000 and December 2017.

Near-term markers in the filing are more modest than the ten-year numbers: the eight core industries grew 4.2% cumulatively in 2017-18, GDP growth was expected to stay above 7% in 2017, and logistics was forecast to grow at a 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020.
Competition is acknowledged only in the abstract — rivals in both the organized and unorganized sectors — with no named competitor and no market share figure anywhere in the excerpts.
The headwinds the filing itself lists are the ones that would hit this business first: slow pace of government projects, working capital crunch, and changes in government policies.

industry.heading: The market it sells into
industry.purpose: Show what the construction market looks like in the filing's own framing, what drives demand, and the headwinds the company itself names.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild builds things the government owns — railway platforms and tracks, bridges and roads — mostly around Mumbai, and it makes its own concrete at a plant in Thane district.
The filing describes the business as two segments and only two: creating infrastructure, and operating a ready mix concrete plant.

Its customers are public bodies — the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, MRVCL, MMRDA and DFCCIL among them — so work arrives through tenders and bids, not sales calls.
The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value, at an issue price the filing leaves as ₹[●].
The money raised is earmarked for working capital requirements (₹1,130 lakhs, or ₹11.30 crore) and general corporate purposes, where the filing does not disclose an amount.
One number frames everything that follows: Indian Railways was 57% of FY2018 revenue, and Western Railway alone accounts for 52% of the orders on hand.

intro.purpose: Orient the reader in plain words: a Mumbai infrastructure contractor that builds government-owned railway works, bridges and roads and makes its own concrete, raising money mainly for working capital.

beats.beat: The issue is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, priced at ₹[●]; a fresh issue raises new money for the company, while an offer for sale lets existing owners sell down, and the split between the two is not stated in the excerpts.
The filing states the face value is ₹10 and that the issue price is ₹[●] times the face value, leaving the multiple blank as well.

The objects of the issue point to money going to the company rather than to a selling shareholder: ₹1,130 lakhs (₹11.30 crore) for working capital requirements, plus general corporate purposes with no disclosed amount.

Working capital is not an abstract object here. Short-term borrowings stood at ₹3,537.35 lakhs (₹35.37 crore) at March 31, 2018, so fresh equity against the working-capital line is the practical purpose of the raise.
Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited is the lead manager to the issue; Bigshare Services Private Limited is the registrar.
No monitoring agency has been appointed to watch the deployment of the proceeds; the filing says the funds are at the discretion of management, monitored by the audit committee.

offer.heading: The offer and what the money is for
offer.purpose: Set out exactly what is being sold, on what terms, who is running the issue, and — plainly — what the filing does not disclose.

beats.beat: Customer concentration is the first risk and the largest. Indian Railways was 57% of FY2018 revenue, and the filing states that loss of Indian Railways as the largest customer would cause a significant dip in revenue.

Revenue depends on winning government tenders awarded to the lowest bidder. The filing says the company's attempts to secure government and PSU projects may not always succeed, and that a failure to obtain new contracts would materially hurt its financial condition.

The order book is not a forecast. The filing says contracts in the order book may be adjusted, cancelled or suspended by clients, and that the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenues or earnings — which matters when Western Railway is 52% of the orders on hand.

The company had negative cash flow in recent financial years, and the filing states that sustained negative cash flow could adversely impact the business, financial condition and results of operations.

₹405.02 lakhs (₹4.05 crore) of unsecured loans were outstanding at March 31, 2018 and are repayable on demand; any demand for repayment could affect cash flow and financial condition. Separately, revenue is concentrated geographically in Mumbai, so an adverse development there hits the whole book.

risks.heading: The five risks that matter
risks.purpose: Give the reader five specific, company-level risks from the filing, each with a number or a named party attached. No more than five.

beats.beat: An Indian IPO is not priced by the issuer alone: the filing has to set out its accounting ratios against listed peers and argue that the price is justified by the comparison.
The number at the centre of that section is missing. The face value is ₹10, the issue price is ₹[●], and the filing says only that the price is ₹[●] times face value.

The peer comparison page compares accounting ratios with peer group companies, but the digest of it carries values without peer names or row labels — 12.39, 28.14, 44.71, and 6,053.05 alongside a face value of 10 — so the peer table itself is not reproducible from the excerpts, and no peer P/E, EPS, NAV or RoNW is captured.

The Basis for Issue Price section does set out per-share and return figures for three years: 4.14, 1.97 and 28.14 for FY2016, FY2017 and FY2018, and a second row at 1.31, 0.63 and 12.59 for the same years.
Because the price is blank and no peer multiple is named in the excerpts, an implied price range cannot be built from this filing. Anything that produced a number here would be invented, not sourced.
One pricing-related disclosure does exist and matters: the company issued equity shares in the 12 months before the filing at a price that may be lower than the issue price.
